title: Problems With Lucy Calkins’ Curriculum Go Beyond Reading—To Writing
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler extends the critique of Lucy Calkins from reading to writing, where Calkins' influence through the Units of Study has been even greater. She traces the approach to a 1980s New Hampshire study and credits Calkins with seeing writing as a process, then argues the curriculum rests on two flawed assumptions. The first is that writing skills can be taught separately from content such as history or science, leaving content-neutral lessons and interchangeable topics. The second is that a workshop model designed for adult writers will work for five-year-olds, who are asked to write at length before they can construct sentences. Wexler's alternative is to embed writing in the core content curriculum and to ease the cognitive burden through explicit instruction and supervised practice starting at the sentence level.
points: Calkins' units teach writing as a content-neutral method, so topics are treated as swappable.
Writing about a subject is a powerful way to build knowledge only once students have a threshold of information about it.
Workshop and flash-drafting approaches underestimate how overwhelming writing is for young children.
Many children need repeated, teacher-guided practice at the sentence level before extended writing.
Wexler's two principles are to embed writing in the core curriculum and to modulate cognitive load with explicit instruction.
quotes: But her approach has rested on two flawed assumptions. The first is that writing skills can and should be taught separately from subjects like history or science—an assumption Calkins and many others have also made about supposed reading comprehension skills like “finding the main idea.

When I interviewed Calkins for a book several years ago, she told me that children should acquire substantive knowledge in their social studies and science classes, but that’s not her focus. “When I’m teaching people to write,” she said, “I’m teaching them a method—I’m teaching them how to do something.

That approach might work for personal essays, but it can run into trouble in units where the goal is to get kids to write “like a scientist” or “like a historian.” Scientists and historians can write the way they do only because they know a lot about their topics.

But writing requires juggling so many different factors—forming letters, choosing and spelling words, organizing thoughts—that it can be overwhelming. Children may become paralyzed, not knowing how to begin. Or they may pour out pages of barely legible and largely incoherent prose.

Writing instruction has enormous potential to build knowledge and literacy, but to unlock its power, two basic principles need to be observed—both of which Calkins overlooks. First, writing activities should be embedded in the content of the core curriculum so that they build the knowledge we want students to acquire. Second, teachers need to modulate the heavy cognitive burden imposed by writing through explicit instruction and supervised practice, beginning at the sentence level if that is what students need.

But writing is really hard. It’s not underestimating students’ abilities to say they need a slower pace and more explicit instruction. Rather, for many students, providing them with those things is the key to unlocking their true potential.
